notes.b: The region studied is the Federative Republic of Brazil, a country so large that it fills about half of a continent. Its position across the tropics shapes almost everything else about it.
points: Brazil is in eastern South America and covers about 8.5 million km2, the world's fifth-largest country by area and about half of South America.

The equator crosses the far north, near the mouth of the Amazon, and the Tropic of Capricorn (the line of latitude south of the equator marking the edge of the tropics) passes close to São Paulo, so most of Brazil is tropical.
It has an Atlantic coastline of about 7,400 km, which is why early settlement and today's biggest cities cluster near the sea.
Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador, but those neighbours are only neighbours, not part of the region studied.
The country has 26 states and the Federal District, and its capital is Brasília.
notes.tip: The capital is Brasília, not Rio de Janeiro or São Paulo. Rio was the capital until 1960, and São Paulo is the largest and richest city.

notes.h: Why Brazil is a continental region
notes.b: A region is an area with something that unites it. Brazil is big enough to be treated like a continent in its own right, and it holds together as one unit.
points: Its continental size: it is larger than most continents' individual countries and contains very different climates, landscapes and economies.
It is a single federal state (a country made of states that share a central government) with one language, Portuguese, surrounded by Spanish-speaking countries, which sets it apart culturally.
It has its own culture and economy, shaped by Portuguese colonisation, African and Indigenous peoples and later immigrants.
It has clear internal regions, the five macro-regions, which let you study how physical, economic and human processes interact inside one country.
notes.tip: Brazilians speak Portuguese, not Spanish. Say so whenever you explain why Brazil is a distinct region.

notes.b: Brazil is divided officially into five macro-regions (large groupings of states). You will use these names in almost every answer, so learn what each is known for.
points: North: the Amazon, the largest region by area and the least populated.
Northeast: the sugar coast and the semi-arid interior called the sertão; it is the poorest region.
Centre-West: the Cerrado (tropical savanna), the soya frontier and the capital, Brasília.
Southeast: São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Minas Gerais; this is the economic core of the country.
South: a cooler region of European immigrant settlement with prosperous farming and industry.
notes.tip: When an exam question asks about regional differences, name the macro-regions and give each one a one-word character, such as North for Amazon or Southeast for core.

notes.b: A sketch map earns marks for an accurate outline and for showing and naming each feature asked for. Learn one example of each feature and exactly where it goes. Names may go on the map or in a key.
points: Outline: a broad northern bulge across the Amazon, an eastward shoulder at the Northeast, then the coast running south-west and the country tapering towards the south.
Relief: outline the Brazilian Highlands (the east-centre, inland from the coast, from the Northeast down to the south) or the Amazon Basin lowland (the north-west and north).

River: draw the Amazon entering in the far west, flowing east past Manaus, where the Rio Negro joins from the north-west, and ending at a wide estuary close to the equator. Mark Marajó Island at the mouth.
Urban centres as dots: São Paulo just inland behind the south-east coast near the Tropic of Capricorn, and Rio de Janeiro on the coast east-north-east of São Paulo.
Agricultural region as an outlined area: the soya region of Mato Grosso in the centre-west, south of the Amazon lowland.

Industrial region as an outlined area: the triangle joining São Paulo, Rio de Janeiro and Belo Horizonte. Other placing cues: Manaus in the centre-north, Brasília in the centre and Salvador on the Northeast coast.
notes.tip: Examiners ask for an outline, a named relief feature shown as an outline, the course of a named river, one or two urban centres and sometimes an outlined agricultural or industrial region. Put coastal cities on the coast and inland cities inland.

notes.b: Six controls explain why Brazil has so many climates inside one country. Each one pushes temperature or rainfall up or down in a particular area.
points: Latitude: most of Brazil lies between the equator and the Tropic of Capricorn, so it gets strong sun and is mostly hot.

The ITCZ (Intertropical Convergence Zone, the belt where winds from north and south meet and air rises to give heavy rain) moves north and south with the overhead sun, so it brings rain to different areas in different seasons.
The south-east trade winds blow in off the warm Atlantic, carrying moist air onto the east coast.
Altitude: the plateau is cooler than the coast because air cools with height.
Relief: the coastal escarpment (a steep slope) forces moist air to rise, cool and drop rain on the seaward side.
Cold fronts from the south reach the South and parts of the Southeast, bringing sudden falls in temperature and sometimes frost.
notes.tip: Physical processes questions ask how climate influences the region or its economy. Name the controls and link each to a specific place, such as the escarpment and the east coast.

notes.b: The North has an equatorial climate (found on or near the equator): hot, wet and with almost no seasons. This is the climate that supports the rainforest.
points: It is hot all year, with Manaus monthly means of about 26-28 degrees C, so the annual temperature range is small.
Manaus gets about 2,300 mm of rain a year, with heavy rain in every month, because strong heating makes warm moist air rise and form storm clouds (convectional rain).
The climate sustains the Amazon rainforest biome, which is dealt with in the Geoecology option.
notes.tip: Not all of Brazil is rainforest. The Amazon biome covers about half the country, so don't describe the whole of Brazil as equatorial.

notes.h: Tropical wet-and-dry climate of the Centre-West
notes.b: The Cerrado has a tropical wet-and-dry (savanna) climate, with a clear rainy summer and a long dry winter. The change comes from the movement of the ITCZ and the overhead sun.
points: The rainy season runs from about October to April, when the ITCZ and the overhead sun move south, so warm moist air rises over the Centre-West.
The dry season runs from about May to September, when the ITCZ has moved north, so the winter is long and dry.
Brasília is the example: it follows this wet and dry pattern, and its altitude of about 1,100 m keeps it milder than the lowlands.
This clear wet season matters for farming, because crops such as soya are planted with the first rains.
notes.tip: Use Brasília as your named example of this climate, and give both seasons with their months.

notes.b: The interior of the Northeast is the driest part of Brazil even though it lies in the tropics. The sertão (the semi-arid Northeast interior) has low and unreliable rain, which is behind many of the region's problems.
points: The sertão gets roughly 250-800 mm a year, falling in a short rainy season and varying greatly from year to year.
It lies in the rain shadow (the dry area on the sheltered side of high ground) of the coastal plateau, so moist air from the Atlantic loses its rain before it arrives.
Sinking air limits convection, and the ITCZ reaches the area only briefly, so there are few chances for heavy rain.
El Niño years (when the Pacific Ocean is unusually warm) bring drought, so the rains can fail altogether.
The officially defined drought-prone area is the drought polygon (Polígono das Secas). A severe drought hit the Northeast from 2012 to 2017.
notes.tip: If asked why the sertão is dry, give at least three causes: rain shadow, sinking air, brief ITCZ presence and El Niño.

notes.b: The east coast is wet while the interior behind it is dry. Winds off the ocean and the shape of the land explain the difference.
points: The south-east trade winds bring moisture off the warm Atlantic, so the air arriving at the coast is already full of water vapour.
Where the air meets the coastal escarpment, such as the Serra do Mar behind the coast of São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro states, it is forced to rise and cool, giving relief rain.
This creates a wet coastal strip that once carried the Atlantic Forest.
The wet coast contrasts with the semi-arid sertão further inland, which lies beyond the rain-giving slopes.
notes.tip: Link this block to the sertão: the escarpment and plateau take the rain on the coast and leave the interior dry.

notes.h: Tropical highland climate of the Southeast
notes.b: In the Southeast, height above sea level matters as much as latitude. The plateau is noticeably cooler than the coast at the same latitude.
points: Temperatures fall with altitude, so the plateau moderates the heat of the tropics.
São Paulo, on the plateau, is cooler than Rio de Janeiro on the coast, which is why the highlands are comfortable for people and suit crops such as coffee.
This cooler climate is one reason the plateau became the centre of settlement, farming and industry.
notes.tip: A good contrast to quote is São Paulo (plateau, cooler) against Rio de Janeiro (coast, hotter).

notes.h: Humid subtropical climate of the South
notes.b: The far south lies furthest from the equator, and it is the only part of Brazil with a real winter. This affects what can be grown.
points: It has four seasons and rain all year, because cold fronts from the south bring rain in every season.
Winter frosts occur, and there is occasional snow in the highlands of Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.
Porto Alegre is the main city of the far south.
The frost risk shaped where coffee is grown, because frost kills the trees. This is why coffee moved north after the frost of 1975, which the coffee notes deal with in full.
notes.tip: Frost in the south is a classic example of a physical problem for farming. Pair it with the 1975 coffee frost if asked.

notes.b: Brazil's climate is not safe or steady. Droughts and floods both cause deaths and damage, and some hazards are linked to El Niño and to forest loss.
points: Droughts in the Northeast are repeated and severe, as in 2012 to 2017.
In 2023 a severe Amazon drought brought the Rio Negro at Manaus to its lowest level on record, in October 2023, stranding river communities.
In May 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul killed more than 170 people and displaced hundreds of thousands, and Porto Alegre was flooded.
In January 2011 floods and landslides in the mountain region of Rio de Janeiro state killed more than 900 people, Brazil's worst natural disaster. Landslides also hit Petrópolis in February 2022.
El Niño links droughts in the north and east to Pacific warming, and deforestation reduces rainfall recycling (the forest returning water to the air), which may make drought worse.
notes.tip: Name a year and a place for each hazard, for example the 2011 mountain region floods or the 2023 Amazon drought.

notes.h: Why climate matters for human activity
notes.b: Climate decides what can be grown, where people live and how energy is produced. Four effects are worth learning.
points: Warm temperatures in the tropics allow two or three crops a year, which raises farm output.
Drought drives migration out of the sertão, because people cannot farm when the rains fail.
Heavy rainfall over much of the country feeds the rivers that power hydroelectricity.
Beaches, sun and warm weather attract tourists, so climate supports the tourist industry.
notes.tip: For a question on how climate influences economic activity, give one effect for farming, one for energy and one for people, each with a place.

notes.h: Latosols, the soils of the Amazon and Cerrado
notes.b: Many people expect tropical soils to be rich because of the lush forest. In fact most Amazon and Cerrado soils are poor, and the reason is climate.
points: Latosols (also called ferralsols or oxisols) are deep, red-yellow soils that cover much of the Amazon and Cerrado.
Heat and heavy rain leach them (wash nutrients out of them), so they are acidic and low in nutrients.
The fertility is held in the living vegetation and its litter, not in the soil, so cleared land loses its fertility fast.
The process that produces these soils, laterisation, is explained in the Geoecology option.
notes.tip: Don't call Amazon soils fertile. Only the várzea and terra preta soils are exceptions.

notes.h: Cerrado soils and how they were improved
notes.b: The Cerrado soils were once thought useless for crops. Science changed that, and now they are a major farming area.
points: Cerrado soils are acidic and high in aluminium, which damages plant roots.
Liming (adding crushed limestone) cuts the acidity, and fertiliser adds nutrients.
EMBRAPA (Brazilian Agricultural Research Corporation, founded 1973) developed these methods.
The result was that infertile savanna became productive farmland, a change that underlies the soya belt covered in the agriculture notes.
notes.tip: Examiners like technology as a factor in farming. EMBRAPA and liming are your named example.

notes.h: Terra roxa and massapê, the fertile soils
notes.b: Two soils explain much of Brazil's farming history. Both are deep and fertile, and each was the base of a famous crop.
points: Terra roxa means purple earth in Portuguese, from its dark red colour. It is deep and fertile.
It weathers from the basalt of the Paraná Plateau in Paraná and São Paulo states, and it was the soil of the coffee boom.
Massapê is a dark, clay-rich, fertile soil found on the humid Northeast coast, in the Zona da Mata (the wet coastal strip around Recife and Salvador).
Massapê was the base of the colonial sugar plantations, which is why sugar grew there first.
notes.tip: Terra roxa comes from basalt on the Paraná Plateau, not from the Amazon. Mixing this up is a known error.

notes.b: Two soils break the rule that Amazon soils are poor. One is natural and one is made by people.
points: Várzea (floodplain) soils are renewed every year by silt left by floods, so they are among the few fertile Amazon soils.
Terra preta (black earth) is dark, fertile soil made by pre-Columbian Amazon peoples (those living there before European contact) by adding charcoal, food waste and pottery.
Terra preta shows that people can improve tropical soils, and not only damage them.
notes.tip: These two are the exceptions to quote when a question says Amazon soils are infertile.

notes.b: Soils can be lost or damaged as well as improved. Three main problems affect Brazilian farmland.
points: Sertão soils are thin and stony, and easily eroded because there is little vegetation to hold them.
Erosion follows forest clearance, because rain then washes away the exposed topsoil.
Old pasture suffers nutrient loss and compaction (being pressed hard by cattle) so grass grows poorly.
Salinisation (a build-up of salt) occurs in irrigated areas where the water evaporates and leaves the salt behind.
notes.tip: For a soil problem question, give the cause and the place: erosion after clearance, salinisation in irrigated areas, thin soil in the sertão.

notes.b: Brazil has six biomes (large natural vegetation regions). They show that Brazil is not all rainforest.
points: Amazon rainforest covers about 49% of Brazil's area, the largest biome.
Cerrado (tropical savanna) covers about 24%, and is often called the world's most biodiverse savanna.
Atlantic Forest covers about 13%, but only about an eighth of the original forest remains because it grew where most Brazilians live.
Caatinga (dry thorn scrub of the sertão) covers about 10% and is found only in Brazil.
Pampa (grassland) covers about 2% and so does the Pantanal (wetland).
notes.tip: Not all of Brazil is rainforest. Quote the shares to show the Amazon is about half and give the Caatinga as a Brazil-only biome.

notes.b: Each biome matches a climate and soil. Link the vegetation to what causes it.
points: The Cerrado has a wet and dry climate and acidic soils, so it supports tropical grassland with scattered trees.
The Caatinga's dry thorn scrub matches the semi-arid climate of the sertão, because only drought-tolerant plants survive there.
The Atlantic Forest grew on the wet east coast fed by the trade winds, and its heavy loss came from settlement and farming along the coast.
The Pantanal is a seasonally flooded wetland, and the Pampa is a grassland in the south where gaúchos herd cattle in Rio Grande do Sul.
notes.tip: A short match of biome to climate earns marks. For example, Caatinga with semi-arid sertão.

notes.b: Relief is the shape of the land. Brazil is mostly old, low or gently rising ground, with five main divisions to learn.
points: The Brazilian Highlands (Planalto) cover the centre, east and south.
The Amazon lowland (basin) lies across the north.
The Guiana Highlands lie on the northern border.
The Pantanal lowland is in the Centre-West, and a narrow coastal plain runs along the Atlantic.
These divisions are the starting point for the sketch map relief feature.
notes.tip: The Andes are not in Brazil. Don't list them as part of Brazil's relief.

notes.b: Brazil sits in the middle of a tectonic plate, which explains why its landscapes are old and quiet.
points: Brazil lies in the centre of the South American plate, far from plate boundaries, so it has no active volcanoes and few strong earthquakes.
The highlands are part of the ancient Brazilian Shield (an old crystalline block of hard rock), once part of Gondwanaland.
Mesosaurus fossils are found in Brazil and southern Africa, evidence that the two were joined.
notes.tip: Brazil has no active volcanoes because it is mid-plate. The Andes are not in Brazil.

notes.b: The Highlands are the main block of high ground. They are old, worn-down and tilted, and this shapes where rivers go.
points: They are old, worn-down plateaus and tablelands, mostly 300-900 m high, shaped over a very long time by weathering and erosion.
They tilt from a high eastern edge towards the interior, so many rivers rise near the coast but flow inland.
This tilt is one reason the Paraná and São Francisco flow away from the nearest sea.
notes.tip: Use the tilt of the plateau to explain river direction in a drainage answer.

notes.b: Behind the coast of the Southeast the land rises steeply. This steep edge has had a big effect on settlement and transport.
points: The Serra do Mar and Serra da Mantiqueira rise steeply behind the coast, so the coastal plain is very narrow.
São Paulo sits on the plateau about 800 m above sea level and about 70 km from the port of Santos.
The slope is a barrier to transport between ports and the plateau, so roads and railways were costly to build.
It also forces moist air to rise, giving the relief rain described under the east coast climate.
notes.tip: Use São Paulo and Santos as your example of the escarpment as a transport barrier.

notes.b: In the south the Highlands are covered by lava. This basalt created the best coffee soil and one of the world's great waterfalls.
points: Thick layers of basalt (a dark volcanic rock) formed from ancient fissure eruptions, flood basalts about 130 million years old.
The basalt weathers into terra roxa, the soil of the coffee boom.
The Iguaçu Falls drop over its basalt edge on the Iguaçu River on the Brazil-Argentina border, about 275 separate falls and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
notes.tip: Say that the Iguaçu Falls are shared with Argentina when you name them.

notes.h: The Amazon lowland and the Guiana Highlands
notes.b: The north has a very different relief from the Highlands. One block is the lowest, flattest part of Brazil, and the other holds its highest peak.
points: The Amazon lowland is a vast, low, flat basin of sedimentary rocks and alluvium (river-deposited sediment), between the Guiana and Brazilian Highlands.
It widens to the west.
The Guiana Highlands lie on the northern border with Venezuela.
Pico da Neblina, about 2,995 m, in Amazonas state, is Brazil's highest peak.
notes.tip: Brazil's highest peak is Pico da Neblina, not Aconcagua, which is in the Andes outside Brazil.

notes.b: The Pantanal is a lowland that floods and drains with the seasons. It is a special type of landscape in Brazil.
points: It is a huge, flat, seasonally flooded depression in the Centre-West, mainly in Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.
It is flooded for several months each wet season, because rivers spill over the flat land.
It is the world's largest tropical wetland.
It extends into Bolivia and Paraguay, so it is a shared feature.
notes.tip: Say the Pantanal extends into Bolivia and Paraguay. Brazil does not hold it alone.

notes.b: The coast has two very different kinds of scenery, hard rock in the Southeast and sand in the Northeast.
points: At Rio de Janeiro, granite domes and steep hills rise by the sea. Sugarloaf Mountain (Pão de Açúcar) is a granite-gneiss dome about 396 m high.
In the Northeast, Lençóis Maranhenses in Maranhão has white sand dunes with rain-filled lagoons.
Both are tourist attractions, which links relief to the tertiary sector.
notes.tip: Name Sugarloaf for hard rock and Lençóis Maranhenses for dunes.

notes.b: Relief decides where people farm, build and travel. Four patterns stand out.
points: The plateau carries most farming, industry and cities, because the land is gently sloping and the climate is cooler.
The escarpment limited early inland settlement and needs costly roads and railways.
The lowland Amazon is sparsely settled, because of dense forest, flooding and difficult access.
Steep coastal hills host favelas (informal housing areas) that are prone to landslides.
notes.tip: For a relief question, give one advantage and one problem for people, each with a place.

notes.b: A river basin is the area drained by a river and its tributaries. Brazil has several enormous ones, and the pattern is shaped by the tilt of the Highlands.
points: The Amazon basin drains the north.
The Paraná-Paraguay basin drains the south and centre.
The São Francisco basin drains the east.
The Tocantins-Araguaia basin is a fourth, flowing north through the Centre-West.
notes.tip: Learn these four basins, with a direction for each: north, south and centre, east, and Centre-West to north.

notes.b: The Amazon is the world's largest river by discharge and basin area. Do not call it the longest, because that is disputed with the Nile.
points: It rises in the Andes of Peru, is about 6,400 km long and has a basin of about 7 million km2, the world's largest.
It carries about a fifth of all the fresh water that rivers deliver to the oceans, and it has over a thousand tributaries.
In Brazil it is called the Solimões until it meets the Rio Negro at Manaus, the Meeting of the Waters, where dark and pale water flow side by side for several kilometres before mixing.
It flows east to the Atlantic near the equator, ending in a wide estuary around Marajó Island rather than a large delta.
Ocean-going ships can reach Manaus, about 1,500 km inland.
notes.tip: The Andes are not in Brazil. The Amazon rises in the Peruvian Andes. Say it ends in an estuary, not a delta.

notes.b: The Amazon is not a simple channel. It floods, it has two kinds of water and it is shaped by the tide at its mouth.
points: The annual flood rises many metres and spreads into the várzea (forest and land flooded by silt-laden white-water rivers).
It also spreads into the igapó (flooded black-water forest).
Black-water rivers such as the Rio Negro are acidic and low in silt, while white-water rivers such as the Solimões are silt-laden from the Andes.
The pororoca (a tidal bore, a wave that travels upstream) occurs at the mouth.
notes.tip: Learn the three terms: várzea, igapó and pororoca. They are easy marks.

notes.b: The Paraná is the main river of the south and centre. Its flow is controlled by dams that supply the Southeast.
points: It rises on the Brazilian Highlands and flows south-west into Argentina and the Río de la Plata.
It is heavily dammed for hydroelectricity.
Itaipu Dam, on the Brazil-Paraguay border and shared by the two countries, began generating in 1984 and is one of the world's largest hydroelectric plants by output.
The Iguaçu Falls are on a tributary.
notes.tip: Say Itaipu is shared with Paraguay, and the Iguaçu Falls with Argentina.

notes.b: The São Francisco brings water to the dry Northeast, which is why it is called the river of national integration.
points: It rises in the Serra da Canastra, Minas Gerais, is about 2,800 km long, flows north through the semi-arid Northeast and turns east to reach the Atlantic between Alagoas and Sergipe.
It is a lifeline for the sertão, because it is one of few permanent water sources in a dry area.
Dams give power, and the Sobradinho Dam forms one of the world's largest artificial lakes by area.
Petrolina (Pernambuco) and Juazeiro (Bahia) face each other across the river and export irrigated grapes and mangoes.
The transposition project, begun in 2007, carries water by canals to the drier states of Ceará, Paraíba, Pernambuco and Rio Grande do Norte.
notes.tip: Use the São Francisco as your example of a river that supports farming in a dry area.

notes.b: Dams supply cheap power, but they also remove land and people from their homes.
points: Itaipu on the Paraná supplies power to the industrial Southeast.
Tucuruí Dam on the Tocantins, Pará (1984), powers aluminium smelting.
Belo Monte Dam on the Xingu, Pará, was completed in 2019.
Belo Monte was opposed by the Kayapó, displaced thousands of people and flooded forest, so the controversy is about the cost to people and nature.
notes.tip: A balanced answer on dams gives a benefit (power) and a cost (displacement, with Belo Monte as the example).

notes.b: Rivers are under pressure from mining and cities. Three examples show the problem.
points: Mercury from illegal gold mining pollutes rivers in Yanomami territory in Roraima, which harms the health of people who eat the fish.
The Rio Doce was polluted by mine waste after the Mariana disaster, which the mining notes explain.
The Tietê at São Paulo is heavily polluted by sewage from the city.
notes.tip: Name the river and the cause for each example: mercury in Yanomami territory, mine waste in the Rio Doce, sewage in the Tietê.

notes.b: Rivers provide transport, food and water, but both floods and droughts can disrupt them.
points: The Amazon is the main highway of the North, because there are few roads in the forest.
Rivers supply fish, and water for irrigation and cities.
Hydroelectricity comes from rivers with a steep fall and a large flow.
Floods and droughts both disrupt river transport, as in the 2023 drought when the Rio Negro fell to a record low.
notes.tip: When asked how drainage influences the economy, cover transport, irrigation and hydroelectricity, with a river for each.

keyTerms.definition: The Intertropical Convergence Zone, a belt where winds from north and south meet and air rises, bringing heavy rain that moves north and south with the overhead sun.
The semi-arid interior of the Northeast, with low and unreliable rain and a drought-prone climate.
The Polígono das Secas, the officially defined drought-prone area of the Northeast interior.
A deep, red-yellow, acidic soil of the Amazon and Cerrado that is low in nutrients because heat and rain have leached it.
A deep, dark red and fertile soil weathered from the basalt of the Paraná Plateau, the soil of the coffee boom.
A dark, clay-rich and fertile soil of the humid Northeast coast, the base of colonial sugar plantations.
Forest and land flooded each year by silt-laden white-water rivers, giving some of the few fertile soils in the Amazon.
Dark fertile soil made by pre-Columbian Amazon peoples by adding charcoal, food waste and pottery.
The dry thorn scrub biome of the sertão, found only in Brazil.
The world's largest tropical wetland, a flat, seasonally flooded depression mainly in Mato Grosso and Mato Grosso do Sul.
A steep slope, such as the Serra do Mar, which forces air to rise and acts as a barrier to transport.
The tidal bore of the Amazon, a wave that travels upstream at the river mouth.

questions.prompt: Draw an outline map of Brazil. On it, show and name a feature of relief, the course of a river, two urban centres and an agricultural region.
questions.model: Draw the outline of Brazil with a broad northern bulge across the Amazon, an eastward shoulder at the Northeast, then the coast running south-west and the country tapering to the south. Relief: outline the Brazilian Highlands as an area in the east-centre of the country, inland from the coast, running from the Northeast down to the south, and label it Brazilian Highlands. River: draw the Amazon as a line entering Brazil in the far west and flowing east past Manaus, where the Rio Negro joins from the north-west, to the Atlantic at a wide estuary close to the equator, and mark Marajó Island at the mouth. Urban centres: put a dot for São Paulo inland, just behind the south-east coast near the Tropic of Capricorn, and a dot for Rio de Janeiro on the coast, east-north-east of São Paulo, and name both. Agricultural region: outline the soya region of Mato Grosso in the centre-west, south of the Amazon lowland, and label it soya, Mato Grosso.
